extracted.intended_audience: general readers and researchers seeking an encyclopedic overview of the X (formerly Twitter) social network
extracted.subtask_description: A comprehensive Wikipedia article summarizing the history, features, policies, usage, and controversies of X (formerly Twitter). It documents product features, platform rules, notable events, and governance changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post character limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Posts were initially limited to 140 characters, changed to 280 characters in 2017. The limitation was removed for subscribed accounts in 2023. From 2023 Twitter Blue users could create posts with up to 4,000 characters in length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: History of evolving length limits is given to explain how posting constraints vary by account type; long-form posting depends on subscription tiers (e.g., Twitter Blue/X Premium).

rubrics_metrics.name: Image description (alt text) availability and length
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions can be added to any uploaded image with a limit of 1000 characters. Images that have a description will feature a badge that says ALT which brings up the description when clicked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originally introduced with smaller caption limits (e.g., 480 characters for image captions in 2016); alt text is available globally (2022) and intended for screen readers and accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tweet attachment counting rules (character counting exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: In 2016 Twitter announced that attachments, links, media such as photos, videos, and the person's handle would no longer count toward the character limit; in 2017 handles were excluded as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains which elements are excluded from character counting to allow longer visible content despite character limits; applies to character-limit enforcement for composing posts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polls: duration and voter anonymity
rubrics_metrics.description: In 2015 Twitter rolled out the ability to attach poll questions to tweets. Polls are open for up to 7 days, and voters are not identified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies maximum poll lifetime and privacy property (anonymous voting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reply visibility and reply controls
rubrics_metrics.description: Users can hide replies to their messages and select who can reply to each of their tweets before sending them: anyone, accounts who follow the post's author, specific accounts, or none.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes author-side controls for narrowing audience of replies and moderating conversation at the time of posting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spaces (social audio) participant limits and creation eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter Spaces is a social audio feature that enables users to host or participate in a live-audio environment called a space. A maximum of 13 people are allowed onstage. The feature was initially limited to users with at least 600 followers, but since October 2021 any Twitter user can create a Space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives both participation caps and the eligibility evolution for creating Spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: t.co URL wrapper requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: All links posted to Twitter use a t.co wrapper. It is only available for links posted to Twitter and not general use. Twitter intended the service to protect users from malicious sites and to use it to track clicks on links within tweets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platform-level automatic URL-shortening/wrapping policy is described, including stated security and analytics purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paid verification / verification marker policy and pricing details
rubrics_metrics.description: The verification marker was included in a premium tier of Twitter Blue introduced on November 9, 2022, priced at US$7.99 per month (later variations existed). Legacy verification status was removed in March 2023; a subscription was required to retain verified status, with organizations charged $1,000 per month plus $50 per affiliate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes real-world problems (impersonation abuses) after initial rollout, temporary suspension, relaunch, and the shifting policy that moved verification to a paid/subscription model with distinct pricing for organizations and affiliates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification required / verified organizations program for advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective April 21, 2023, Twitter requires companies to participate in the verified organizations program to purchase advertising on the platform, although companies that spend at least $1,000 on advertising per month automatically receive membership in the program at no additional cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes a commercial eligibility rule tying verification/organization status to advertising capability and an automatic-entry threshold based on ad spend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising policy on political and misleading content
rubrics_metrics.description: In October 2019 Twitter announced it would stop running political ads on its ad platform effective November 22, 2019. The company reversed the ban in August 2023, publishing criteria governing political advertising which do not allow the promotion of false or misleading content and requiring advertisers to comply with laws, with compliance being the sole responsibility of the advertiser.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarizes the timeline and the key constraints in current policy: (1) political advertising allowed under published criteria, (2) prohibition on false or misleading content, (3) legal compliance required of advertisers. The article notes the company did not publish full guidelines at times and applied ad bans selectively (e.g., Russia-related ad ban).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ban on advertising that contradicts scientific consensus (climate change example)
rubrics_metrics.description: In April 2022, Twitter announced a ban on 'misleading' advertisements that go against 'the scientific consensus on climate change'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An example of content-specific advertising restrictions; the article notes Twitter did not provide full guidelines but indicated decisions would be made with help from 'authoritative sources'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Super Follows / Subscriptions for creators (pricing and features)
rubrics_metrics.description: In 2021 the company opened applications for premium subscription options called Super Follows, letting eligible accounts charge $2.99, $4.99 or $9.99 per month. In 2023 Super Follows was rebranded as 'subscriptions', allowing users to publish exclusive long-form posts and videos for their subscribers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes creator monetization features, pricing tiers at launch, and the later pivot to support long-form content as a strategic product move to compete with platforms like Substack.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tips, Ticketed Spaces and crypto payouts
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter tested a Tip Jar feature allowing users to send monetary tips to certain accounts and announced support for tipping via bitcoin (integrating Strike). Ticketed Spaces let hosts charge between $1 and $999 for access. In April 2022 Twitter announced a partnership with Stripe to pilot cryptocurrency payouts for limited users; eligible creators could receive earnings in USD coin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarizes available creator payment options, pricing ranges for Ticketed Spaces, early integrations with crypto payment providers, and the pilot nature of some payment features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hashflags (sponsored/custom hashtag emoji)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hashflags are special hashtags that automatically generate a custom emoji next to them for a period of time. Hashflags may be generated by Twitter themselves or purchased by corporations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes hashflags are time-limited, can be platform-generated or commercially purchased, and used in promotional/brand contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fleets temporal nature and removal
rubrics_metrics.description: Fleets were a stories feature launched in November 2020 that could contain text and media and were only accessible for 24 hours after they were posted; they were removed in August 2021.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of an ephemeral-content product lifecycle: introduction, intended use-case (encourage regular tweeting), and removal due to low adoption by target users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counts and metrics displayed on posts (likes, reposts/retweets, replies, quote tweet counters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Counters for likes, retweets, and replies appear next to the respective buttons in timelines; since 2020 quote tweets have their own counter. Counters for likes and reposts exist on a post's standalone page too.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains what engagement metrics are surfaced on the platform and that quote tweets are tracked separately for engagement measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of tweet content types (Pear Analytics categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pear Analytics (2009) categorized tweet content into News (3.6%), Spam (3.8%), Self-promotion (6%), Pointless babble (40%), Conversational (38%), and Pass-along value (8.7%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides an empirical taxonomy used in early research to describe typical tweet content; the article notes alternative characterizations (e.g., 'social grooming') and the interpretive nature of these categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithmic personalization and documented bias effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter's machine learning recommendation algorithm personalized 99% of users' feeds (introduced 2016) by displaying tweets deemed relevant to users' past preferences; studies and reports cited in the article found amplification effects (e.g., amplifying right-leaning politics) and measurable shifts in user behavior and beliefs when switching from chronological to algorithmic feeds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarizes evaluative findings about algorithmic curation: the algorithm amplifies some content types, can change engagement and political attitudes, and has been subject to external audit and academic scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: User content and behavior controls (mute, block, lists)
rubrics_metrics.description: Users can mute users they do not wish to interact with, block accounts from viewing their posts, and remove accounts from their followers list. Users can group posts together by topic or type by use of hashtags and use Lists (public or private) to follow curated account collections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the suite of user-side moderation and organization tools available to control exposure and curate content streams.
